nameStory: This honeysuckle gets its name from Tatary, a historical region in Central Asia where it naturally grows. European botanists first described it from specimens collected in this vast area that stretched across parts of modern-day Russia, Mongolia, and Central Asia. The name connects this invasive shrub to its far-off homeland, thousands of miles from the New England forests it now colonizes.
description: Tatarian honeysuckle is a deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall with an upright, somewhat spreading form. It's an invasive species from Asia that has established itself throughout New England's forests and disturbed areas. The plant produces paired flowers in spring followed by bright red berries in summer, and its opposite leaves give it a neat, organized appearance that helps distinguish it from many native shrubs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pink to white tubular flowers appear in pairs at the base of leaves in late spring, each about an inch long with five petals that flare out into a trumpet shape. The flowers have a sweet, pleasant fragrance and feel papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, oval leaves grow in opposite pairs along the stem and feel somewhat thick and leathery. They're typically 1-3 inches long with a blue-green color and prominent veining that you can feel by running your finger along the surface.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red or orange berries appear in summer, growing in pairs where the flowers once bloomed. The berries are about 1/4 inch across, feel firm and smooth, and often persist into fall when they become somewhat wrinkled.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature stems develop a distinctive shredding, fibrous bark that peels in long strips, revealing lighter brown wood underneath. Young twigs are smooth and hollow when broken, making a satisfying snap.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, upright shrubs with multiple stems arising from the base, often creating thickets in favorable locations. The branching pattern is very regular and symmetrical, giving it a somewhat formal appearance even in wild settings.

habitat: Tatarian honeysuckle thrives in a wide variety of habitats from forest edges and clearings to roadsides and disturbed areas. It's particularly common in partially shaded locations with moist, well-drained soils but tolerates both full sun and deeper shade. You'll often find it forming dense colonies beneath mature trees or along woodland borders throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Paired pink or white tubular flowers bloom in May and early June, filling the air with sweet fragrance. New leaves emerge bright green and feel tender compared to their summer texture.
seasonality.summer: Bright red berries ripen in July and August while the foliage reaches full size and develops its characteristic blue-green color. This is when the plant is most easily identified by its paired berries.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow before dropping, and berries often persist, becoming somewhat shriveled but still visible. The plant's structure becomes more apparent as surrounding vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: The distinctive peeling, fibrous bark becomes the main identification feature, along with the opposite branching pattern and any persistent dried berries. Hollow twigs snap cleanly when broken.

funFact: Despite producing thousands of attractive red berries that birds love to eat, Tatarian honeysuckle is basically junk food for wildlife—the berries are much lower in fat and nutrients compared to native alternatives, potentially weakening birds during critical migration periods when they need high-energy foods.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other invasive honeysuckles like Morrow's and Amur honeysuckle, but Tatarian honeysuckle's flowers and berries grow in distinct pairs rather than clusters. Remember: 'Tatarian twins'—everything comes in pairs, from flowers to berries to the way leaves attach to stems.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the sweet fragrance and pretty flowers fool you—this is one of New England's most problematic invasive shrubs. It was originally planted as an ornamental in the 1700s and 1800s but has since escaped cultivation and outcompetes native understory plants, fundamentally altering forest ecosystems.
compareHints: Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries. It's much larger and more robust than native species, and lacks the more delicate, woodland appearance of natives like American fly-honeysuckle. The hollow twigs also distinguish it from most native honeysuckles which have solid or pithy stems.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
